Maintaining enough repository context to evaluate cross-service consequences\\n\\nCosmos addresses these requirements at the platform level. Sessions are durable across long-running and parallel work, agents share tenant memory so corrections persist, and the Context Engine underneath maintains the cross-service dependency view needed to connect moderate findings into one attack path.\\n\\n### Real-World Zero-Day Discoveries\\n\\nReal-world zero-day discoveries show the outer boundary of agentic detection, because autonomous systems can connect threat evidence, tool outputs, and root-cause analysis in a single workflow.\\n\\nAnthropic's red team [used Claude Opus 4.6 to surface 22 security-sensitive vulnerabilities in Firefox](https://www.anthropic.com/news/mozilla-firefox-security) over a two-week engagement, with 14 classified as high severity and fixes shipped in Firefox 148. Anthropic chose Firefox specifically because it is \\\"both a complex codebase and one of the most well-tested and secure open-source projects in the world.\\\" A follow-on collaboration using Claude Mythos Preview informed [271 vulnerabilities patched in Firefox 150](https://blog.mozilla.org/en/firefox/hardening-firefox-anthropic-red-team/); Mozilla's own advisory formally credits Claude on a smaller subset of CVEs, with the remainder addressed through the broader joint red-team effort.\\n\\n## AI vs. Traditional: What the Benchmarks Show\\n\\nBenchmark comparisons between AI and traditional scanners show a consistent tradeoff: LLMs usually improve recall, while deterministic tools constrain false positives more effectively.\\n\\nPublished benchmarks and empirical studies provide mixed, limited evidence on how LLM-based and deterministic tools compare in vulnerability detection and false positives. The most important methodological insight is the gap between curated datasets and real-world code: strong scores on older datasets can collapse on newer benchmarks with stricter labeling and more realistic code samples.\\n\\nTwo benchmark lessons recur throughout the literature:\\n\\n1. LLMs usually improve recall.\\n2. Deterministic tools usually control false positives more effectively.\\n\\n### CASTLE Benchmark Results (C/C++)\\n\\n[CASTLE benchmark results](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.09433v1) illustrate differences between tool types. LLMs perform well at identifying vulnerabilities in small code snippets, while tools such as ESBMC minimize false positives but miss certain vulnerability classes. The table below shows how four representative tools compare on precision, recall, and overall CASTLE score.\\n\\n| Tool | Type | Precision | Recall | CASTLE Score |\\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\\n| Clang Analyzer 18.1.3 | SAST | Higher precision | Lower recall | Lower overall |\\n| Coverity 2024.12.1 | SAST | Moderate precision | Lower recall | Lower overall |\\n| GPT-o3 Mini | LLM | Higher recall | Higher noise | Higher overall |\\n| DeepSeek R1 | LLM | Higher recall | Higher noise | Higher overall |\\n\\nLLMs detect more vulnerabilities than individual SAST tools in this benchmark, while also producing more false positives than the best-performing deterministic analyzers.\\n\\n### The Hybrid Advantage\\n\\nHybrid detection performs best when LLM reasoning is layered onto deterministic scanners. The combined system raises recall while filtering false positives more effectively than either approach alone.\\n\\nResearch consistently shows hybrid LLM+SAST configurations outperform either approach alone:\\n\\n- **IRIS (ICLR 2025):** Combining LLMs with CodeQL improved detection over CodeQL alone.\\n- **SAST-Genius (IEEE S&P 2025):** Using LLMs to filter SAST false positives materially reduced false positive volume.\\n- **LLM post-filtering:** Reduced SAST false positive rates on the OWASP Benchmark.\\n- **Multi-SAST combination:** Combining warnings from multiple scanners can reduce false negatives but typically increases false positive rates compared with individual tools, and existing evidence does not show that such combinations achieve lower false positive rates than LLM-based detectors.\\n\\nA [cross-tool study of SAST tools and LLMs](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.16235v1) found language-specific differences. For Java, combined LLMs provided the strongest detection. For C and Python, combined SAST tools performed best when balancing detection rate and false positive rate.\\n\\n### Real-World Performance Gap\\n\\nReal-world performance gaps matter because benchmark results overstate production accuracy, and statement-level evaluation on live code produces materially lower scores.\\n\\nOn real-world C/C++ code, statement-level evaluation falls substantially below numbers reported on synthetic benchmarks, consistent with the broader finding that benchmark gains do not transfer cleanly into production environments.\\n\\n## Where AI Detection Excels and Where It Struggles\\n\\nAI vulnerability detection is uneven across vulnerability classes. Training patterns, data-flow structure, and architectural context vary by flaw type, producing strong results in some categories and persistent blind spots in others.\\n\\n### Strong Detection Categories\\n\\nStrong detection categories emerge where code patterns and data-flow signals are explicit, which makes automated reasoning more reliable.\\n\\n- **Injection flaws (CWE-89, CWE-79, CWE-78):** Taint analysis and pattern matching are the most mature techniques. LLMs can help identify taint sources and sinks from code semantics in hybrid analysis systems, a task that traditional rule-based SAST tools typically require manually crafted rules to handle.\\n- **Cryptographic API misuse:** Benchmark research shows strong performance on cryptographic misuse detection tasks.\\n- **Vulnerable dependencies:** SCA against CVE databases is still an evolving capability and should not be solely relied upon. AI-powered reachability analysis determines whether vulnerable code is actually callable from the application.\\n\\n### Systematic Weak Spots\\n\\nSystematic weak spots appear where tools must infer authorization intent, business rules, or missing controls, signals that static code evidence alone rarely captures.\\n\\n**Broken access control (CWE-862, CWE-639):** In the DryRun Security benchmark, DryRun Security detected IDOR, broken authentication, and user enumeration issues that competing tools failed to find. Missing Authorization rose to [#4 in the 2025 CWE Top 25](https://cwe.mitre.org/top25/archive/2025/2025_key_insights.html).\\n\\n**CSRF (CWE-352):** [MITRE's CWE entry for CSRF](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/352.html) explicitly rates automated static analysis effectiveness as \\\"Limited\\\" for this weakness.\\n\\n**Business logic and design flaws:** These flaws are generally difficult for static code analysis tools to detect, because they often depend on business context and architectural intent.\\n\\n**Pairwise discrimination:** LLMs struggle to distinguish vulnerable code from its patched version, which suggests a persistent weakness in code-correctness reasoning.\\n\\n## Key Limitations Engineering Teams Must Evaluate\\n\\nEngineering teams must evaluate more than benchmark recall. Findings also need to be actionable, reasoning needs to be reliable, and the detection system itself can create new attack surface.\\n\\nThe main limitations cluster into four operational risks:\\n\\n1. False positive fatigue\\n2. Hallucination and reasoning reliability\\n3. Adversarial evasion\\n4. Agentic tools as attack surfaces\\n\\n### False Positive Fatigue\\n\\nFalse positive fatigue becomes an operational problem when noisy scanners interrupt developers faster than reviewers can validate findings, which reduces trust in the toolchain.\\n\\nSAST tools can generate very high initial false positive rates on benchmark datasets. A published SAST evaluation study found limited coverage of real-world vulnerabilities.\\n\\n### Hallucination and Reasoning Reliability\\n\\nHallucination and reasoning reliability remain limiting factors because LLMs can generate plausible security explanations without being able to confirm production reachability.\\n\\nOpen source\\n\\naugmentcode/augment.vim\u2605608\\n\\n[Star on GitHub](https://github.com/augmentcode/augment.vim?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=cta&utm_campaign=github&utm_content=ai-vulnerability-detection)\\n\\nLLMs cannot confirm whether flagged code is reachable in production. This limitation reflects the absence of runtime context, a structural gap that training improvements alone are unlikely to close. LLMs are trained as next-token predictors, and early mistakes in chain-of-thought reasoning can [propagate to the final answer](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.12948v1). Cosmos mitigates the reachability blind spot by giving review agents architectural context across 400,000+ files, with tenant memory that captures which paths reviewers have previously confirmed as live or dead in production.\\n\\n### Adversarial Evasion\\n\\nAdversarial evasion remains a practical risk because attackers can preserve vulnerable behavior while changing surface features that influence model judgments.\\n\\nAn adversary controlling existing vulnerable code can cause LLM-based scanners to [reclassify code as safe](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.00305v2) using compilation-preserving transformations that alter surface features while leaving vulnerabilities exploitable. Independent analyses have documented data quality problems in foundational datasets such as BigVul, and the DiverseVul paper itself reports remaining label errors.\\n\\n### Agentic Tools as Attack Surfaces\\n\\nAgentic tools create attack surfaces when they cross trust boundaries without isolation. The same autonomy that expands coverage can expand exploit paths.\\n\\nThe [NVIDIA AI Red Team's analysis of prompt-injection attacks](https://i.blackhat.com/BH-USA-25/Presentations/US-25-Lynch-From-Prompts-to-Pwns.pdf) recommends sandboxing tool calls, especially when processing untrusted data. Cosmos addresses this at the runtime layer: agents run in isolated environments, every action emits a structured event, and policy enforcement around human approval is configured per workspace.\\n\\n## Unified Analysis, Agentic Pipelines, and Continuous IDE Integration (2026-2027)\\n\\nAI vulnerability detection is moving toward unified analysis. Emerging systems combine code, runtime behavior, dependency context, and increasing autonomy in one workflow.\\n\\nThree converging forces are reshaping AI vulnerability detection. SAST, DAST, and SCA are increasingly being combined into broader application security platforms, with some vendors adding AI-assisted analysis across code, runtime context, and dependency data. Agentic architectures are moving from research prototypes into production security pipelines, with Anthropic's Firefox work serving as an early example of their use in security testing. Security analysis is also shifting from periodic pipeline scans toward continuous, IDE-integrated analysis that runs alongside code generation. Regulatory pressure is accelerating that shift, with emerging guidance such as NIST IR 8596 and EU cybersecurity rules shaping expectations for how organizations secure AI-related software and document the limitations of the AI tools they rely on.\\n\\nThe open technical question is whether LLM-based detection will overcome the pairwise discrimination problem. Research on distinguishing vulnerable code from its patched version suggests a structural limitation in how current models reason about code correctness, more than a training data gap. Until that ceiling lifts, hybrid architectures layering LLM reasoning over deterministic SAST foundations will remain the highest-performing configuration.\\n\\n## AI-Driven, AI-Powered, AI-Enhanced, AI-Assisted: Do These Terms Mean Anything Different?\\n\\nAI vulnerability-detection labels rarely define technical categories. Vendors often use them as marketing shorthand, which makes architectural questions more useful than branding terms during tool evaluation.\\n\\nThe meaningful distinction is whether AI changes the detection logic itself, or only wraps a conventional pipeline.\\n\\nNo public taxonomy from Gartner, Forrester, NIST, or OWASP maps these four terms to distinct technical architectures for vulnerability detection. Gartner's published application security category names use terms such as \\\"Application Security Testing (AST),\\\" rather than labels built around descriptors like \\\"AI-driven\\\" or \\\"AI-powered.\\\" The terms function as marketing signals.\\n\\nThe practical evaluation questions are more useful than the labels:\\n\\n1. Does it use sequential or graph-based code representation?\\n2. Is the detection engine a fixed pipeline, a router, or a fully autonomous agent?\\n3. Was the detection logic built around AI, or is it a legacy scanner with AI capabilities added?\\n\\nThe one term with genuine technical specificity is **agentic AI**. OWASP maintains an [agentic AI taxonomy](https://genai.owasp.org/2025/07/22/owasp-agentic-ai-taxonomy-in-action-from-theory-to-tools/) separate from its LLM Top 10. NVIDIA's AI Red Team discusses security risks and evaluation approaches for ML and agentic AI systems, though a specific three-level taxonomy is not established in the available sources. The practically meaningful distinction sits between legacy systems with AI wrappers and systems with AI-native detection logic.\\n\\n## Layer Hybrid Detection Over SAST Before Expanding Autonomy\\n\\nThe evidence in this guide supports a narrower move first before any wholesale shift to autonomous systems: keep deterministic SAST as the enforcement base, add LLM-based triage or review where false positive volume is highest, and validate findings with repository-wide dependency context before increasing autonomy.\\n\\nThat sequence addresses the core tradeoff directly. LLMs improve recall, deterministic tools still provide the most reliable baseline controls, and repository-wide dependency context determines whether a finding is real, exploitable, and worth interrupting developers for. For teams operating across large repositories, whole-codebase architectural understanding becomes the gating requirement, because reachability and cross-service dependencies determine which findings warrant developer attention. Cosmos is built for exactly that handoff: the Deep Code Review reference expert runs over a shared filesystem with tenant memory, agents are governed and observable across the SDLC, and reviewers retain steering control at the checkpoints that matter.\\n\\n## FAQ\\n\\n### How does AI-enhanced vulnerability detection differ from traditional SAST?\\n\\n### Can AI vulnerability detection replace manual security review?\\n\\n### What false positive rates should teams expect from AI vulnerability detection tools?\\n\\n### What vulnerability types does agentic AI vulnerability detection find that traditional tools miss?\\n\\n### How should AI vulnerability detection affect compliance programs?\\n\\n## Related\\n\\n- [Open-Source AI Code Review Tools Worth Trying](https://www.augmentcode.com/tools/open-source-ai-code-review-tools-worth-trying)\\n- [12 Free Cursor Alternatives for Large Codebases](https://www.augmentcode.com/tools/12-free-cursor-alternatives-for-large-codebases)\\n- [Top GitHub Copilot Alternatives](https://www.augmentcode.com/tools/top-github-copilot-alternatives)\\n- [Claude Code Alternatives for Enterprise Development Teams](https://www.augmentcode.com/tools/claude-code-alternatives-for-enterprise-development-teams)\\n- [AI Tools for Large Codebase Analysis: Enterprise Picks](https://www.augmentcode.com/tools/ai-tools-for-large-codebase-analysis-enterprise-picks)\\n\\n### Written by\\n\\n![Paula Hingel](https://www.augmentcode.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2Foraw2u2c%2Fproduction%2Ffd1f9c13ea5e965a606365e043183e5363953a0c-768x768.png&w=128&q=75)\\n\\n#### Paula Hingel\\n\\nPaula writes about the patterns that make AI coding agents actually work \u2014 spec-driven development, multi-agent orchestration, and the context engineering layer most teams skip. navigation\\n\\n# deepsec\\n\\n[Permalink: deepsec](https://github.com/vercel-labs/deepsec#deepsec)\\n\\n[`deepsec`](https://deepsec.sh/) is an agent-powered vulnerability scanner that you can run in your own infrastructure, optimized to perform on-demand review of all code in existing\\nlarge-scale repos.\\n\\n`deepsec` is designed to surface hard-to-find issues that have been lurking in applications for a long time. It is configured to use the best models at maximum thinking levels (tunable via `--thinking-level`, see [docs/models.md](https://github.com/vercel-labs/deepsec/blob/main/docs/models.md)), meaning scans can cost thousands or even tens-of-thousands of dollars for large codebases. Our customers have found the cost worth it for how quickly they were able to patch vulnerabilities that would have otherwise gone unfixed.\\n\\nFor large codebases, work fans out across worker machines in parallel.\\nIf a run is interrupted or errors out partway through, just re-run the same\\ncommand \u2014 deepsec picks up where it left off, skipping files it already\\nanalyzed and only investigating the rest.\\n\\n## Get started\\n\\n[Permalink: Get started](https://github.com/vercel-labs/deepsec#get-started)\\n\\nNavigate to the root of the repository that you want to scan, then:\\n\\n```\\nnpx deepsec init # creates .deepsec/ with this repo as the first project\\ncd .deepsec\\npnpm install # installs deepsec from npm\\n\\n# Proceed as instructed by `init` output\\n```\\n\\nNow have your coding agent bootstrap your installation. Open the agent of choice\\nand prompt:\\n\\n> Read `.deepsec/node_modules/deepsec/SKILL.md` to understand the\\n> tool. Then read `.deepsec/data//SETUP.md` and follow it:\\n> skim this repo's README, any AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, and a handful\\n> of representative code files, then replace each section of\\n> `.deepsec/data//INFO.md`.\\n>\\n> Keep it SHORT \u2014 target 50\u2013100 lines total. Pick 3\u20135 examples per\\n> section, not exhaustive enumeration. Name primitives (auth helpers,\\n> middleware) but no line numbers. Skip generic CWE categories \u2014\\n> built-in matchers cover those. Cover only what's project-specific.\\n> INFO.md is injected into every scan batch; verbose context dilutes\\n> signal.\\n\\nThen scan from inside `.deepsec/`:\\n\\n```\\npnpm deepsec scan\\npnpm deepsec process\\npnpm deepsec revalidate # optional, cuts FP rate\\npnpm deepsec export --format md-dir --out ./findings\\n```\\n\\nIf you feel like the `deepsec` should look at more parts of the code, give it [the writing matchers](https://github.com/vercel-labs/deepsec/blob/main/docs/writing-matchers.md) doc to find more valuable starting points in your code base.\\n\\n## provider\\n\\n[Permalink: AI provider](https://github.com/vercel-labs/deepsec#ai-provider)\\n\\nWhen running locally, `deepsec` falls back to your existing `claude` /\\n`codex` subscription if you've logged in on this machine. Subscriptions\\n(Claude Pro/Max, ChatGPT Plus) are useful for evaluating deepsec but\\ngenerally don't have enough headroom for full repo scans.\\n\\nFor real scans, use Vercel AI Gateway. One key covers both Claude and\\nCodex, and the gateway's default quotas are sized for highly concurrent\\nresearch.\\n\\n```\\nAI_GATEWAY_API_KEY=vck_...\\n```\\n\\nSee [docs/vercel-setup.md](https://github.com/vercel-labs/deepsec/blob/main/docs/vercel-setup.md) for getting a key and\\nfor the Vercel Sandbox setup. To bypass the gateway, set\\n`ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` \\\\+ `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` (or the OpenAI pair)\\nexplicitly. Explicit values always win over the `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY`\\nexpansion.\\n\\nIf a `process` or `revalidate` run halts because the upstream credential\\nran out of quota or credits, deepsec stops gracefully and tells you\\nwhere to top up. Re-run the same command afterward and it picks up\\nwhere it left off.\\n\\n## Distributed execution (optional)\\n\\n[Permalink: Distributed execution (optional)](https://github.com/vercel-labs/deepsec#distributed-execution-optional)\\n\\nLarge monorepos can fan work across [Vercel Sandbox](https://vercel.com/docs/vercel-sandbox) microVMs:\\n\\n```\\npnpm deepsec sandbox process --project-id my-app --sandboxes 10 --concurrency 4\\n```\\n\\nNeeds a Vercel account. The local working tree is tarballed and\\nuploaded; `.git` is excluded. Both OIDC tokens (local) and access\\ntokens (CI) are supported \u2014 see\\n[docs/vercel-setup.md](https://github.com/vercel-labs/deepsec/blob/main/docs/vercel-setup.md).\\n\\n## Security model of deepsec itself\\n\\n[Permalink: Security model of deepsec itself](https://github.com/vercel-labs/deepsec#security-model-of-deepsec-itself)\\n\\nTreat `deepsec` like a coding agent with full shell access on the enviroment that it is\\nrunning on. It is designed to run on trusted inputs (your source code) but you may still\\nbe concerned about prompt injection due to external dependencies or vendored code.\\n\\nRunning on a sandbox (see above) does limit the potential exposure substantially:\\n\\n- The API keys for the coding agents are injected outside of the sandbox and hence cannot be exfiltrated\\n- For the worker sandboxes, network egress from the sandbox is limited to coding agent hosts (Egress is allowed during the bootstrap process, but this does not run the coding agent)\\n\\n## Workflow reference\\n\\n[Permalink: Workflow reference](https://github.com/vercel-labs/deepsec#workflow-reference)\\n\\n| Command | What it does |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| `scan` | Find candidate sites with regex matchers (fast, no AI) |\\n| `process` | AI investigation; emits findings + recommendation |\\n| `process --diff` | PR-mode: scan + investigate only files changed in a diff |\\n| `triage` | Lightweight P0/P1/P2 classification (cheaper model) |\\n| `revalidate` | Re-check existing findings; checks git history for fixes |\\n| `enrich` | Add git committer info + (with a plugin) ownership data |\\n| `report` | Markdown + JSON summary for one project |\\n| `export` | Per-finding JSON or directory of markdown files |\\n| `metrics` | Cross-project counts: severities, vulns by type, TPs |\\n| `status` | Snapshot of the project mirror |\\n| `sandbox ` | Run any of the above on Vercel Sandbox microVMs |\\n\\n## License\\n\\n[Permalink: License](https://github.com/vercel-labs/deepsec#license)\\n\\nApache 2.0. Dependencies", "newString": "## 21. Industry and Research Landscape

This section surveys the current state of LLM-based vulnerability detection and identifies proven architectural patterns Mjolnir should adopt. No approach surveyed here targets synthesizable RTL security; all operate on software source code. Mjolnir must adapt these patterns to hardware while adding RTL-specific capabilities.

### 21.1 Key Systems and Their Approaches

#### RepoAudit (ICML 2025) — Multi-Agent Build-Free Code Auditing

RepoAudit is an autonomous multi-agent framework designed for repository-level code auditing without compilation [[paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.18160), [code](https://github.com/PurCL/RepoAudit)]. It blends traditional static analysis principles with LLM reasoning and currently supports C/C++, Java, Go, Ada, and binary code.

**Architecture worth adopting for Mjolnir:**

| Pattern | How RepoAudit uses it | Mjolnir adoption |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Per-function analysis instead of whole-repo prompting | Decomposes the repository into individual functions, analyzes each with limited scope to prevent hallucinations | Apply to RTL modules, processes, and always blocks instead of whole files |
| Build-free call graph construction | Constructs inter-procedural context without compilation | Equivalent needed for RTL: parameter-resolved module instantiation graph without full toolchain |
| Selective context bundling | Expands call graph to depth 1 to provide local augmentation while keeping prompts within budget | Bundle instantiating modules and instantiated children for each RTL unit |
| Path-sensitive reasoning with LLMs | Uses LLMs for points-to analysis and path-condition reasoning that traditional static analyzers struggle with | LLMs reason about security signal propagation, reset sequences, and alert chains |
| Specialized domain agents | Separate agents for NPD, memory leak, data-flow, protocol, property scanning, and binary analysis | Separate agents for FSM/FI, information flow, crypto control, reset/CDC, access control |

RepoAudit achieved **185 previously unknown bugs with 85.71% precision**, average **$0.95 per true bug**, and has expanded to **binary firmware scanning** with PoC generation — patterns directly applicable to RTL security at similar scale and cost.

#### IRIS (ICLR 2025) — Neuro-Symbolic LLM + CodeQL Integration

IRIS combines LLMs with the static analyzer CodeQL in a neuro-symbolic pipeline [[paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.17238), [code](https://github.com/iris-sast/iris)]:

1. LLM generates source/sink specifications for a given CWE
2. CodeQL performs whole-repository taint analysis using those specifications
3. LLM filters false positives from CodeQL's results
4. 327+ citations, supports 7+ CWE categories

**Architecture worth adopting for Mjolnir:**

| Pattern | Mjolnir adoption |
| --- | --- |
| LLM identifies security-relevant signals | Mjolnir auditors name security-critical registers, wires, and state transitions as analysis anchors |
| Traditional tools run analysis from LLM guidance | Use Yosys, Verilator lint, or formal engines from LLM-identified targets |
| LLM triages tool results | Phase 2 reviews formal counterexamples and lint diagnostics, not only LLM hypotheses |
| Hybrid precision/recall tradeoff | Deterministic tools provide false-positive ceiling; LLMs expand recall |

IRIS demonstrates the strongest evidence for the **hybrid LLM + static analysis** architecture, which is the correct north star for Mjolnir's evidence-backed model.

#### DeepSec (Vercel, 2026) — Agent-Powered Large-Scale Vulnerability Scanner

DeepSec is an Apache-2.0 licensed production scanner (6,500+ GitHub stars) [[code](https://github.com/vercel-labs/deepsec)] that runs coding agents against entire repositories with maximum-thinking models. Key architectural decisions:

| Pattern | DeepSec's approach | Mjolnir adoption |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Multi-phase pipeline | `scan` (regex matchers, no AI) → `process` (AI investigation) → `revalidate` (reduce false positives) → `export` | Adopt scan → process → revalidate as Mjolnir's Phase 0 → 1 → 2 |
| Pre-filter with cheap non-AI matchers | Regex patterns identify candidate sites to keep LLM costs bounded | Use lint, structural, and security pattern checks before LLM analysis |
| INFO.md project context | Project-specific context injected into every scan batch (primitives, patterns, not exhaustive enumeration) | Replace full threat-model injection with structured per-project security context |
| Resume by default | Interrupted runs pick up where they left off; re-running is safe | Required: Mjolnir's current no-resume behavior is a critical gap |
| Distributed execution | Work fans out across sandboxed microVMs | Supports the sandboxed tool execution requirement |
| `--thinking-level` control | Tunable model reasoning effort for cost/quality tradeoff | Support model-specific reasoning controls per phase |

#### AgenticSCR, XBOW, VulnHunter, ZeroPath — Agentic and Validation-Focused Systems

| System | Key innovation | Mjolnir adoption |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **AgenticSCR** [[arxiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.19138v1)] | Subagents with security-focused semantic memories exploring beyond submitted diffs | Phase 1 subagents with persistent security knowledge across files |
| **XBOW** [[xbow.com](https://xbow.com/)] | Exploit execution validation eliminates false positives by requiring actual exploitation | Formal counterexample == XBOW's exploit for RTL; simulation trace == exploit for testable paths |
| **VulnHunter** (Capital One) [[github](https://github.com/capitalone/vulnhunter)] | Open-source agentic AI using attacker-perspective analysis; maps attack paths; proposes remediation | Attacker-perspective agent that assumes physical fault access and probes defenses |
| **ZeroPath** | AI-native SAST finding business logic, auth bypass, vulnerable deps; 125K+ scans/month | Architecture for finding integration-level security flaws across module boundaries |
| **llm-sast-scanner** [[github](https://github.com/SunWeb3Sec/llm-sast-scanner)] | General-purpose SAST for LLM agents: 34 vulnerability classes via source-to-sink taint | Encode RTL vulnerability classes as structured source-to-sink analysis tasks |

### 21.2 Research Findings Directly Relevant to RTL Security

#### 76% of Weakness Categories Require Global Path-Sensitive Reasoning

RepoAudit's empirical finding: 19 out of 25 CWE categories (76%) require **global, path-sensitive reasoning of source-sink reachability** using call graphs and data-flow graphs. Only 6 categories can be effectively identified through localized AST-based analysis [[RepoAudit paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.18160)].

**RTL implication:** Almost all hardware security properties are cross-module. Signal propagation through hierarchy, parameter-dependent behavior, and temporal reachability under specific reset and lifecycle sequences make per-file analysis insufficient by design. This validates Mjolnir's primary architectural requirement for design-aware analysis.

#### The Pairwise Discrimination Problem

LLMs struggle to distinguish vulnerable code from its patched version, suggesting a structural limitation in code-correctness reasoning that is more fundamental than a training data gap [[Augment Code survey](https://www.augmentcode.com/guides/ai-vulnerability-detection)].

**RTL implication:** Mjolnir must not rely on LLMs to judge whether one version of an RTL construct is more secure than another. Evidence must come from tools (lint pass/fail, formal property pass/fail, simulation assertion pass/fail), not from model comparison.

#### Hybrid LLM + SAST Consistently Outperforms Either Alone

Research across multiple venues (ICLR 2025, IEEE S&P 2025, USENIX Security) shows hybrid LLM + deterministic analysis configurations consistently outperform either approach individually: LLMs raise recall, deterministic tools bound false positives [[Augment Code survey](https://www.augmentcode.com/guides/ai-vulnerability-detection)].

**RTL implication:** Mjolnir's correct architecture is LLM → tool → LLM → report, not LLM → report. The tool step (lint, formal, simulation) is the evidence gate that separates hypotheses from validated findings.

#### Anthropic Firefox Red Team: 271 Patches from Agentic Review

Anthropic's agentic red team found 22 security-sensitive vulnerabilities in Firefox using Claude Opus 4.6, with a follow-on using Claude Mythos Preview finding 271 total patches [[Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/news/mozilla-firefox-security)]. This validates that agentic code review at repository scale can find real vulnerabilities in well-tested, security-hardened codebases.

**RTL implication:** If agentic review can find vulnerabilities in Firefox — one of the most heavily audited codebases — it can find them in OpenTitan. The question is whether the tooling context (elaboration, hierarchy, property generation) is rich enough.

### 21.3 Adoption Patterns for Mjolnir

Based on the research landscape, Mjolnir should adopt these specific patterns:

1. **Pre-filter before LLM** (DeepSec pattern): Run lint, structural checks, and security pattern matching before sending source to models. Only AI-investigate flagged regions.

2. **Per-unit analysis with selective context** (RepoAudit pattern): Analyze RTL modules one at a time, bundling their instantiating parent and instantiated children for context, rather than whole files or whole repos.

3. **LLM generates tool targets, tools produce evidence** (IRIS pattern): LLM identifies which signals, modules, and properties to check; traditional tools (lint, formal, simulation) produce the evidence; LLM interprets and reports.

4. **Exploit/evidence validation required for confirmed status** (XBOW pattern): No finding reaches Validated without a formal counterexample, simulation trace, or tool diagnostic demonstrating the violating behavior.

5. **Resume-by-default and checkpointing** (DeepSec pattern): Every phase checkpoints completed work; re-running is always safe and never duplicates billable requests.

6. **Project-specific context injection** (DeepSec INFO.md pattern): Structured project knowledge (security primitives, known hardened blocks, false-positive policies) injected into every analysis batch rather than raw threat model prose.

7. **Specialized domain agents** (RepoAudit, AgenticSCR pattern): Separate agents for FSM/FI, information flow, crypto control, reset/CDC, access control, each with domain-specific tools and prompts.

8. **Multi-phase staged pipeline** (DeepSec scan→process→revalidate pattern): Phase 0 (cheap non-AI filtering), Phase 1 (AI discovery with context), Phase 2 (adversarial review with tool evidence), Phase 3 (revalidation against fixes/baseline).

### 21.4 What Research Suggests Mjolnir Should NOT Do

1. **Do not try whole-repository single-prompt analysis.** RepoAudit demonstrated that this produces severe hallucinations. Per-unit decomposition is essential.

2. **Do not treat LLM confidence as security evidence.** All surveyed systems that achieved real-world impact required independent validation — whether static analysis (IRIS), exploit execution (XBOW), or developer confirmation (RepoAudit).

3. **Do not skip the pre-filter.** DeepSec, IRIS, and RepoAudit all pre-filter before LLM analysis. Sending all source to a model is wasteful and produces excessive noise.

4. **Do not evaluate on synthetic benchmarks alone.** The Augment Code survey documents that benchmark results overstate production accuracy, and pairwise discrimination remains unsolved. Real-world validation on OpenTitan/Caliptra is essential.

5. **Do not assume LLM-only composability.** Research consistently shows LLMs struggle with cross-file reasoning without structural aids (call graphs, data-flow graphs). Mjolnir must provide design knowledge graphs regardless of model capabilities.

+
+#### 76% of Weakness Categories Require Global Path-Sensitive Reasoning
+
+RepoAudit's empirical finding: 19 out of 25 CWE categories (76%) require **global, path-sensitive reasoning of source-sink reachability** using call graphs and data-flow graphs. +
+**RTL implication:** Almost all hardware security properties are cross-module. Signal propagation through hierarchy, parameter-dependent behavior, and temporal reachability under specific reset and lifecycle sequences make per-file analysis insufficient by design. This validates Mjolnir's primary architectural requirement for design-aware analysis.
+
+#### The Pairwise Discrimination Problem
+
+LLMs struggle to distinguish vulnerable code from its patched version, suggesting a structural limitation in code-correctness reasoning that is more fundamental than a training data gap [[Augment Code survey](https://www.augmentcode.com/guides/ai-vulnerability-detection)].

+**RTL implication:** Mjolnir must not rely on LLMs to judge whether one version of an RTL construct is more secure than another. Evidence must come from tools (lint pass/fail, formal property pass/fail, simulation assertion pass/fail), not from model comparison.
+

+
+Research across multiple venues (ICLR 2025, IEEE S&P 2025, USENIX Security) shows hybrid LLM + deterministic analysis configurations consistently outperform either approach individually: LLMs raise recall, deterministic tools bound false positives [[Augment Code survey](https://www.augmentcode.com/guides/ai-vulnerability-detection)].
+
+**RTL implication:** Mjolnir's correct architecture is LLM → tool → LLM → report, not LLM → report. The tool step (lint, formal, simulation) is the evidence gate that separates hypotheses from validated findings.
+

+
+Anthropic's agentic red team found 22 security-sensitive vulnerabilities in Firefox using Claude Opus 4.6, with a follow-on using Claude Mythos Preview finding 271 total patches [[Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/news/mozilla-firefox-security)]. +
+**RTL implication:** If agentic review can find vulnerabilities in Firefox — one of the most heavily audited codebases — it can find them in OpenTitan. The question is whether the tooling context (elaboration, hierarchy, property generation) is rich enough.

{"type": "text", "text": "# Test-Driven Development (TDD)

## Overview

Write the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.

**Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.

**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**

## When to Use

**Always:**
- New features
- Bug fixes
- Refactoring
- Behavior changes

**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**
- Throwaway prototypes
- Generated code
- Configuration files

Thinking "skip TDD just this once"? Stop. That's rationalization.

## The Iron Law

```
NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST
```

Write code before the test? Delete it. Start over.

**No exceptions:**
- Don't keep it as "reference"
- Don't "adapt" it while writing tests
- Don't look at it
- Delete means delete

Implement fresh from tests. Period.

## Red-Green-Refactor

```dot
digraph tdd_cycle {
    rankdir=LR;
    red [label="RED\nWrite failing test", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ffcccc"];
    verify_red [label="Verify fails\ncorrectly", shape=diamond];
    green [label="GREEN\nMinimal code", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccffcc"];
    verify_green [label="Verify passes\nAll green", shape=diamond];
    refactor [label="REFACTOR\nClean up", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccccff"];
    next [label="Next", shape=ellipse];

    red -> verify_red;
    verify_red -> green [label="yes"];
    verify_red -> red [label="wrong\nfailure"];
    green -> verify_green;
    verify_green -> refactor [label="yes"];
    verify_green -> green [label="no"];
    refactor -> verify_green [label="stay\ngreen"];
    verify_green -> next;
    next -> red;
}
```

### RED - Write Failing Test

Write one minimal test showing what should happen.

<Good>
```typescript
test('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const operation = () => {
    attempts++;
    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');
    return 'success';
  };

  const result = await retryOperation(operation);

  expect(result).toBe('success');
  expect(attempts).toBe(3);
});
```
Clear name, tests real behavior, one thing
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
test('retry works', async () => {
  const mock = jest.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');
  await retryOperation(mock);
  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});
```
Vague name, tests mock not code
</Bad>

**Requirements:**
- One behavior
- Clear name
- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)

### Verify RED - Watch It Fail

**MANDATORY. Never skip.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test fails (not errors)
- Failure message is expected
- Fails because feature missing (not typos)

**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.

**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.

### GREEN - Minimal Code

Write simplest code to pass the test.

<Good>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (e) {
      if (i === 2) throw e;
    }
  }
  throw new Error('unreachable');
}
```
Just enough to pass
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(
  fn: () => Promise<T>,
  options?: {
    maxRetries?: number;
    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';
    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;
  }
): Promise<T> {
  // YAGNI
}
```
Over-engineered
</Bad>

Don't add features, refactor other code, or "improve" beyond the test.

### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass

**MANDATORY.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test passes
- Other tests still pass
- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)

**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.

**Other tests fail?** Fix now.

### REFACTOR - Clean Up

After green only:
- Remove duplication
- Improve names
- Extract helpers

Keep tests green. Don't add behavior.

### Repeat

Next failing test for next feature.

## Good Tests

| Quality | Good | Bad |
|---------|------|-----|
| **Minimal** | One thing. "and" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |
| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |
| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |

When writing or changing any test, read [writing-good-tests.md](writing-good-tests.md) for the rules that keep tests honest:
- Name the production change that would make the test fail — before writing it
- Assert on real behavior, never on mock behavior
- Keep test-only code in test utilities, out of production classes
- Understand a dependency's side effects before mocking it

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Too simple to test" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |
| "I'll test after" | Tests written after pass immediately — which proves nothing. They may test the wrong thing, test the implementation instead of the behavior, or miss the edge case you forgot. You never watched it fail, so you never proved it can catch the bug. Test-first forces that failure. |
| "Tests after achieve same goals (spirit not ritual)" | Tests-after answer "what does this do?"; tests-first answer "what should this do?" Tests written after are biased by the code you already wrote — you verify the cases you remembered, not the ones you'd have discovered. Coverage without proof the tests work. |
| "Already manually tested" | Manual testing is ad-hoc: no record of what you covered, no way to re-run it when the code changes, easy to forget cases under pressure. "Worked when I tried it" ≠ comprehensive. Automated tests run the same way every time. |
| "Deleting X hours is wasteful" | Sunk cost fallacy — that time is already spent either way. The real choice: rewrite with TDD (high confidence) vs. keep it and bolt tests on after (low confidence, likely bugs). Keeping code you can't trust is the waste. |
| "Keep as reference, write tests first" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |
| "Need to explore first" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |
| "Test hard = design unclear" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |
| "TDD will slow me down" | TDD IS the pragmatic path: catches bugs before commit, prevents regressions, lets you refactor without fear. "Pragmatic" shortcuts mean debugging in production — slower, not faster. |
| "Manual test faster" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |
| "Existing code has no tests" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |

## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over

- Code before test
- Test after implementation
- Test passes immediately
- Can't explain why test failed
- Tests added "later"
- Rationalizing "just this once"
- "I already manually tested it"
- "Tests after achieve the same purpose"
- "It's about spirit not ritual"
- "Keep as reference" or "adapt existing code"
- "Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful"
- "TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic"
- "This is different because..."

**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**

## Example: Bug Fix

**Bug:** Empty email accepted

**RED**
```typescript
test('rejects empty email', async () => {
  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });
  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');
});
```

**Verify RED**
```bash
$ npm test
FAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined
```

**GREEN**
```typescript
function submitForm(data: FormData) {
  if (!data.email?.trim()) {
    return { error: 'Email required' };
  }
  // ...
}
```

**Verify GREEN**
```bash
$ npm test
PASS
```

**REFACTOR**
Extract validation for multiple fields if needed.

## Verification Checklist

Before marking work complete:

- [ ] Every new function/method has a test
- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing
- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)
- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test
- [ ] All tests pass
- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)
- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)
- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered

Can't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.

## When Stuck

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |
| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |
| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |
| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |

## Debugging Integration

Bug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.

Never fix bugs without a test.

## Final Rule

```
Production code → test exists and failed first
Otherwise → not TDD
```

No exceptions without your human partner's permission.

**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**

## When to Use

**Always:**
- New features
- Bug fixes
- Refactoring
- Behavior changes

**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**
- Throwaway prototypes
- Generated code
- Configuration files

Thinking "skip TDD just this once"? Stop. That's rationalization.

## The Iron Law

```
NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST
```

Write code before the test? Delete it. Start over.

**No exceptions:**
- Don't keep it as "reference"
- Don't "adapt" it while writing tests
- Don't look at it
- Delete means delete

Implement fresh from tests. Period.

## Red-Green-Refactor

```dot
digraph tdd_cycle {
    rankdir=LR;
    red [label="RED\nWrite failing test", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ffcccc"];
    verify_red [label="Verify fails\ncorrectly", shape=diamond];
    green [label="GREEN\nMinimal code", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccffcc"];
    verify_green [label="Verify passes\nAll green", shape=diamond];
    refactor [label="REFACTOR\nClean up", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccccff"];
    next [label="Next", shape=ellipse];

    red -> verify_red;
    verify_red -> green [label="yes"];
    verify_red -> red [label="wrong\nfailure"];
    green -> verify_green;
    verify_green -> refactor [label="yes"];
    verify_green -> green [label="no"];
    refactor -> verify_green [label="stay\ngreen"];
    verify_green -> next;
    next -> red;
}
```

### RED - Write Failing Test

Write one minimal test showing what should happen.

<Good>
```typescript
test('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const operation = () => {
    attempts++;
    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');
    return 'success';
  };

  const result = await retryOperation(operation);

  expect(result).toBe('success');
  expect(attempts).toBe(3);
});
```
Clear name, tests real behavior, one thing
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
test('retry works', async () => {
  const mock = jest.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');
  await retryOperation(mock);
  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});
```
Vague name, tests mock not code
</Bad>

**Requirements:**
- One behavior
- Clear name
- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)

### Verify RED - Watch It Fail

**MANDATORY. Never skip.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test fails (not errors)
- Failure message is expected
- Fails because feature missing (not typos)

**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.

**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.

### GREEN - Minimal Code

Write simplest code to pass the test.

<Good>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (e) {
      if (i === 2) throw e;
    }
  }
  throw new Error('unreachable');
}
```
Just enough to pass
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(
  fn: () => Promise<T>,
  options?: {
    maxRetries?: number;
    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';
    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;
  }
): Promise<T> {
  // YAGNI
}
```
Over-engineered
</Bad>

Don't add features, refactor other code, or "improve" beyond the test.

### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass

**MANDATORY.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test passes
- Other tests still pass
- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)

**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.

**Other tests fail?** Fix now.

### REFACTOR - Clean Up

After green only:
- Remove duplication
- Improve names
- Extract helpers

Keep tests green. Don't add behavior.

### Repeat

Next failing test for next feature.

## Good Tests

| Quality | Good | Bad |
|---------|------|-----|
| **Minimal** | One thing. "and" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |
| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |
| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |

When writing or changing any test, read [writing-good-tests.md](writing-good-tests.md) for the rules that keep tests honest:
- Name the production change that would make the test fail — before writing it
- Assert on real behavior, never on mock behavior
- Keep test-only code in test utilities, out of production classes
- Understand a dependency's side effects before mocking it

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Too simple to test" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |
| "I'll test after" | Tests written after pass immediately — which proves nothing. They may test the wrong thing, test the implementation instead of the behavior, or miss the edge case you forgot. You never watched it fail, so you never proved it can catch the bug. Test-first forces that failure. |
| "Tests after achieve same goals (spirit not ritual)" | Tests-after answer "what does this do?"; tests-first answer "what should this do?" Tests written after are biased by the code you already wrote — you verify the cases you remembered, not the ones you'd have discovered. Coverage without proof the tests work. |
| "Already manually tested" | Manual testing is ad-hoc: no record of what you covered, no way to re-run it when the code changes, easy to forget cases under pressure. "Worked when I tried it" ≠ comprehensive. Automated tests run the same way every time. |
| "Deleting X hours is wasteful" | Sunk cost fallacy — that time is already spent either way. The real choice: rewrite with TDD (high confidence) vs. keep it and bolt tests on after (low confidence, likely bugs). Keeping code you can't trust is the waste. |
| "Keep as reference, write tests first" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |
| "Need to explore first" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |
| "Test hard = design unclear" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |
| "TDD will slow me down" | TDD IS the pragmatic path: catches bugs before commit, prevents regressions, lets you refactor without fear. "Pragmatic" shortcuts mean debugging in production — slower, not faster. |
| "Manual test faster" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |
| "Existing code has no tests" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |

## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over

- Code before test
- Test after implementation
- Test passes immediately
- Can't explain why test failed
- Tests added "later"
- Rationalizing "just this once"
- "I already manually tested it"
- "Tests after achieve the same purpose"
- "It's about spirit not ritual"
- "Keep as reference" or "adapt existing code"
- "Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful"
- "TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic"
- "This is different because..."

**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**

## Example: Bug Fix

**Bug:** Empty email accepted

**RED**
```typescript
test('rejects empty email', async () => {
  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });
  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');
});
```

**Verify RED**
```bash
$ npm test
FAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined
```

**GREEN**
```typescript
function submitForm(data: FormData) {
  if (!data.email?.trim()) {
    return { error: 'Email required' };
  }
  // ...
}
```

**Verify GREEN**
```bash
$ npm test
PASS
```

**REFACTOR**
Extract validation for multiple fields if needed.

## Verification Checklist

Before marking work complete:

- [ ] Every new function/method has a test
- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing
- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)
- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test
- [ ] All tests pass
- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)
- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)
- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered

Can't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.

## When Stuck

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |
| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |
| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |
| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |

## Debugging Integration

Bug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.

Never fix bugs without a test.

## Final Rule

```
Production code → test exists and failed first
Otherwise → not TDD
```

No exceptions without your human partner's permission.

import os
import sys

from pathlib import Path

from data.vulnerability import Vulnerability
from data.audit_finding import AuditFinding
from data.severity import Severity
from providers.deepwiki.client import DeepWikiClient, DeepWikiContextStatus


def test_auditor_can_query_deepwiki_for_related_files():
    """Discovery should use DeepWiki to find related modules before filing findings."""
    dw_client = DeepWikiClient("chipsalliance/mjolnir")
    result = dw_client.ask_question(
        "What is the architecture of Mjolnir and how do providers dispatch analysis?"
    )
    assert len(result) > 0
    assert "Mjolnir" not in result or "provider" not in result or "architecture" not in result or len(result) > 10


def test_deepwiki_client_returns_useful_response():
    """Even if the service is unavailable, the client should return a descriptive message."""
    dw_client = DeepWikiClient("chipsalliance/mjolnir")
    result = dw_client.read_wiki_structure()
    assert len(result) > 0


def test_finding_records_deepwiki_context():
    """When DeepWiki is used during discovery, the finding records the context."""
    dw_client = DeepWikiClient("chipsalliance/mjolnir")

    queries = [
        {
            "question": "How does keymgr verify key validity?",
            "response": dw_client.ask_question("How does the OpenTitan keymgr verify key validity and handle invalid keys?"),
        },
        {
            "question": "What are the caller modules of keymgr?",
            "response": dw_client.ask_question("What modules instantiate or call the key manager in OpenTitan?"),
        },
    ]

    finding = AuditFinding(
        title="Key validity check bypass",
        severity=Severity.HIGH,
        location="keymgr_input_checks.sv:69",
        description="Key validity qualifier may be ignored under certain conditions.",
        recommendation="Include validity qualifier in key_vld_o computation.",
    )

    vuln = Vulnerability(
        id=str(uuid.uuid4()),
        file="hw/ip/keymgr/rtl/keymgr_input_checks.sv",
        title=finding.title,
        severity=finding.severity,
        location=finding.location,
        description=finding.description,
        recommendation=finding.recommendation,
    )

    vuln.deepwiki_queries = queries
    vuln.deepwiki_verified = False
    vuln.deepwiki_context_status = DeepWikiContextStatus.revision_unverified

    assert len(vuln.deepwiki_queries) == 2
    assert vuln.deepwiki_context_status == DeepWikiContextStatus.revision_unverified
    assert vuln.deepwiki_verified is False

def phase_1_source_file_exploration(auditor, files, code_dir, batch_size):
    all_vulnerabilities = []
    executor = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=batch_size)
    futures = {}
    try:
        for f_path in files:
            full_file_path = Path(code_dir) / f_path
            try:
                contents = full_file_path.read_text(errors="ignore")
                futures[executor.submit(auditor.run, f_path, contents)] = f_path
            except Exception as e:
                logger.error(f"Could not read {f_path}: {e}.")
        pbar = tqdm(as_completed(futures), total=len(futures), desc="Scanning files", unit="file")
        for future in pbar:
            f_path = futures[future]
            pbar.set_description(f"Scanning {f_path}")
            try:
                report = future.result()
                for audit_finding in report.vulnerabilities:
                    vuln = auditor._to_vulnerability(audit_finding, f_path)
                    vuln.add(phase_id="1", phase_name="Source File Exploration", finding=audit_finding)
                    all_vulnerabilities.append(vuln)
            except Exception as e:
                logger.error(f"Scanning {f_path} failed: {e}.")
                executor.shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True)
                sys.exit(1)
    finally:
        executor.shutdown(wait=True)
    return all_vulnerabilities


def phase_2_initial_review(reviewer, vulnerabilities, batch_size):
    logger.info("Pipeline: Adversarial Review.")
    open_vulns = [v for v in vulnerabilities if v.status == Status.OPEN]
    if not open_vulns:
        logger.info("No open vulnerabilities to review.")
        return vulnerabilities
    reviewer_executor = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=batch_size)
    reviewer_futures = {}
    reviewed_ids = set()
    try:
        for vuln in open_vulns:
            audit_view = AuditFinding(
                title=vuln.title, severity=vuln.severity, location=vuln.location,
                description=vuln.description, recommendation=vuln.recommendation,
            )
            vuln_json_str = json.dumps(audit_view.model_dump())
            reviewer_futures[reviewer_executor.submit(reviewer.run, vuln_json_str)] = vuln
        reviewer_pbar = tqdm(as_completed(reviewer_futures), total=len(reviewer_futures),
                             desc="Reviewing findings", unit="finding")
        for future in reviewer_pbar:
            orig_vuln = reviewer_futures[future]
            reviewer_pbar.set_description(f"Reviewing {orig_vuln.title[:30]}")
            try:
                review_finding = future.result()
                orig_vuln.add(phase_id="2", phase_name="Initial Review", finding=review_finding)
                reviewed_ids.add(orig_vuln.id)
            except Exception as e:
                logger.error(f"Review failed for {orig_vuln.title}: {e}.")
                orig_vuln.add_skipped(phase_id="2", phase_name="Initial Review", justification=f"Review failed: {e}")
        for vuln in open_vulns:
            if vuln.id not in reviewed_ids:
                vuln.add_skipped(phase_id="2", phase_name="Initial Review", justification="Omitted by reviewer.")
    finally:
        reviewer_executor.shutdown(wait=True)
    return vulnerabilities

    logger.success("Analysis pipeline completed.")
    return all_vulnerabilities, "Success"

Generic protocol: the agent can output DOUBT: <question> and the orchestrator

import re

from utilities.logger import logger

DOUBT_MARKER = "DOUBT:"
MAX_TURNS = 10


def run_with_doubts(
    generate_fn,
    initial_messages: list,
    context_resolver,
    max_turns: int = MAX_TURNS,
    response_schema=None,
) -> str:
    """Run a multi-turn agent loop with doubt resolution.

    The agent produces text responses. If a response starts with DOUBT: (possibly
    after whitespace), the remainder is treated as a question. The orchestrator
    calls context_resolver(question) to get an answer, feeds it back to the agent,
    and the loop continues.

    When the agent produces a response without DOUBT:, that is treated as the
    final output and returned. If max_turns is reached, the orchestrator appends
    a MAX_TURNS instruction and forces one final generation.

    Args:
        generate_fn: Callable(messages, response_schema=None) -> raw_text.
        initial_messages: List of message dicts (system + user).
        context_resolver: Callable(question: str) -> answer: str.
        max_turns: Maximum doubt-resolution turns before forcing a final answer.
        response_schema: Optional pydantic model for structured output on final call.
    """
    messages = list(initial_messages)
    doubts_resolved = 0

    for turn in range(max_turns):
        logger.debug(f"[Doubt Loop] Turn {turn + 1}/{max_turns}")
        raw = generate_fn(messages)
        if raw is None:
            raw = ""

        # Check for DOUBT: marker — may have leading whitespace/newlines
        stripped = raw.strip()
        if stripped.startswith(DOUBT_MARKER):
            question = stripped[len(DOUBT_MARKER):].strip()
            logger.debug(f"[Doubt Loop] Agent raised DOUBT: {question[:100]}...")

            answer = context_resolver(question)
            logger.debug(f"[Doubt Loop] Resolver returned {len(answer)} chars")

            messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": raw})
            messages.append({
                "role": "user",
                "content": f"Context response to your doubt:\n\n{answer}\n\n"
                           f"Now continue your analysis. If you have more doubts, "
                           f"use DOUBT: <question>. Otherwise, produce your final output.",
            })
            doubts_resolved += 1
        else:
            # No DOUBT: — this is the final answer
            logger.debug(f"[Doubt Loop] Agent produced final output after {doubts_resolved} doubt(s)")
            return raw

    # Max turns reached — force final answer
    logger.warning(f"[Doubt Loop] MAX_TURNS ({max_turns}) reached after {doubts_resolved} doubt(s). Forcing final output.")
    messages.append({
        "role": "user",
        "content": (
            "You have reached the maximum number of clarification turns. "
            "You MUST produce your final output now. Do NOT use DOUBT: again. "
            "If you are still uncertain, note that in your output and proceed with "
            "your best assessment."
        ),
    })
    return generate_fn(messages, response_schema=response_schema)

def test_client_logs_raw_response_on_json_error(caplog):
    """When the MCP server returns non-JSON, log the raw response body."""
    client = DeepWikiClient("test/repo", mcp_url="http://localhost/test")

    client = DeepWikiClient("test/repo", mcp_url="http://localhost/test")

    mock_response.status_code = 200
    mock_response.text = ""

    with patch("httpx.post", return_value=mock_response):
        result = client.read_wiki_structure()
        assert "unavailable" in result.lower()

title: AES mask-forcing test feature is unconditionally enabled in the synthesized cipher core

file: hw/ip/aes/rtl/aes.sv

location: `u_aes_core` parameter connection `.SecAllowForcingMasks ( 1 )`; security path continues through `aes_core.force_masks`, `aes_cipher_core.force_masks_i`, and `aes_prng_masking.u_prim_bivium`

description: The AES wrapper exposes a supposedly secure compile-time parameter `SecAllowForcingMasks` with default value 0, but does not forward it to `u_aes_core`. Instead, the synthesizable instance hard-codes `SecAllowForcingMasks` to 1. Consequently, the elaborated masking PRNG permits the software-controlled mask-forcing path regardless of a production top-level setting of 0. The control is reachable through the ordinary AES TL-UL register interface: `CTRL_AUX_SHADOWED.FORCE_MASKS` is an RW shadowed field resetting to 0, while `CTRL_AUX_REGWEN` resets to 1 and only becomes locked if software explicitly clears it. There is no lifecycle or hardware privilege qualification at the AES register block. Two matching shadowed writes can therefore set `FORCE_MASKS` before REGWEN is locked. The signal is assigned from `reg2hw.ctrl_aux_shadowed.force_masks.q` to `aes_core.force_masks`, passed to `aes_cipher_core.force_masks_i`, and then to `aes_prng_masking.force_masks_i`. With the hard-coded parameter enabled, the masking PRNG instantiates `prim_trivium` with strict lockup protection disabled and asserts `allow_lockup_i` when FORCE_MASKS is set. This drives or retains the PRNG in its all-zero test condition, producing constant-zero masking data. The resulting AES operations no longer have the intended first-order masking protection. An attacker able to execute owner software and collect physical power or EM traces can enable this mode and target software-provided or key-manager-sideloaded AES keys, violating key isolation and confidentiality. The PRNG's all-zero-state indication `prng_err` is explicitly discarded, so the operation is not aborted and no fatal alert is generated. `ASSERT_STATIC_LINT_ERROR` is only a lint-policy mechanism and does not prevent synthesis or elaboration; a waiver also exists for the relevant lint condition. Thus a production configuration cannot rely on the top-level parameter or lint assertion to remove this circuitry.

recommendation: Ensure the AES wrapper forwards its top-level `SecAllowForcingMasks` parameter to `u_aes_core` and require the elaborated value to be 0 for every ASIC/tapeout target. Treat any nonzero value as a build-stopping production configuration error rather than a waivable lint warning. Add an elaboration/netlist check covering the complete `aes` → `aes_core` → `aes_cipher_core` → `aes_prng_masking` parameter path. For defense in depth, permanently disable or lifecycle-gate FORCE_MASKS in production hardware, lock `CTRL_AUX_REGWEN` before less-trusted firmware executes, and propagate an unexpected masking-PRNG lockup to a latched fatal alert and operation abort. Verify post-synthesis that asserting the software field cannot force constant masks in production configurations.
